questions.stem: Which three values are needed to calculate a heat energy change?

options.text: Mass heated, temperature change and specific heat capacity
options.explanation: Those three multiply together to give the heat energy change in joules.

options.text: Volume, time and temperature change
options.explanation: Time never enters the expression; volume must first be turned into a mass.

options.text: Mass, boiling point and specific heat capacity
options.explanation: The change in temperature matters, not the boiling point.

options.text: Moles, temperature change and density
options.explanation: Moles belong to the molar enthalpy step, not to the heat energy change itself.

questions.stem: What does a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/g/°C mean for water?

options.text: 1 g of water needs 4.18 J to rise by 1 °C
options.explanation: The definition ties one gram and one degree to the stated energy.

options.text: 1 litre of water needs 4.18 J to boil
options.explanation: The definition concerns a 1 °C rise for 1 g, not boiling a litre.

options.text: Water warms by 4.18 °C for every joule supplied
options.explanation: That inverts the ratio; many joules are needed for a single degree.

options.text: Water releases 4.18 J when it freezes
options.explanation: Freezing involves a different energy change altogether.

questions.stem: 100 cm3 of dilute solution is warmed. What mass should the calculation use?

options.text: 100 g, because the solution is assumed to have the density of water
options.explanation: The 1 g/cm3 assumption makes the volume reading double as the mass.

options.text: 50 g, because half the solution is water
options.explanation: No such split exists in the assumption set; the whole solution behaves like water.

options.text: The mass of the dissolved solid only
options.explanation: Everything in the cup is warmed, not just the solute.

options.text: The mass cannot be found without a balance
options.explanation: The density assumption removes the need to weigh the solution.

questions.stem: A temperature rises from 25 °C to 37 °C. What ΔT goes into the expression?

options.text: 12 °C, the difference between final and initial readings
options.explanation: Subtracting 25 from 37 gives the change the expression needs.

options.text: 37 °C, the final temperature itself
options.explanation: The expression wants the change, not the endpoint.

options.text: 62 °C, the two readings added
options.explanation: Adding temperatures has no physical meaning here.

options.text: 25 °C, the starting temperature
options.explanation: The starting reading alone says nothing about the size of the change.

questions.stem: Why can a temperature change in °C be used unchanged in the expression?

options.text: A change of one degree Celsius equals a change of one kelvin
options.explanation: The two scales differ by a fixed offset, so differences are identical on both.

options.text: Celsius and kelvin are the same scale with different names
options.explanation: The scales have different zero points; only their step sizes match.

options.text: The expression works in Fahrenheit too
options.explanation: Fahrenheit degrees are a different size, so the expression would break.

options.text: Specific heat capacity has no units
options.explanation: It carries J/g/°C, which is why the temperature unit matters.

questions.stem: State the three quantities needed to calculate the heat energy change.
questions.modelAnswer: The heat energy change is found from the mass heated, the temperature change and the specific heat capacity.

questions.stem: State the specific heat capacity assumed for the solutions in these calculations.
questions.modelAnswer: Solutions are assumed to share water's specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/g/°C.

questions.stem: Explain why a temperature change in degrees Celsius can be used directly in the Q expression without converting to kelvin.
questions.modelAnswer: A temperature difference has the same size in degrees Celsius as in kelvin, so the value of the temperature change substituted into Q is unchanged.

questions.stem: A mixture of mass 100 g warms by 8 degrees Celsius. State the three inputs that should be substituted into the Q expression.
questions.modelAnswer: Substitute m = 100, the specific heat capacity 4.18 and the 8-degree rise for the temperature difference, then multiply them to get Q in joules.

questions.stem: A calculation gives Q = 3135 J and the temperature rose. What is the final quoted answer?

options.text: -3.14 kJ, because the exothermic change makes the value negative
options.explanation: The rise shows energy left the chemicals, so the negative sign applies before converting to kilojoules.

options.text: +3.14 kJ, because energy calculations are always positive
options.explanation: Sizes are positive but enthalpy changes carry the direction as a sign.

options.text: -3135 kJ, because joules convert directly
options.explanation: Dividing by 1000 was skipped; the number is a kilojoule conversion error.

options.text: 3135 kJ, because the sign is optional
options.explanation: The sign is chemistry, not decoration, and the unit is wrong.

questions.stem: Why must the enthalpy change for a combustion always be negative?

options.text: Combustion always releases heat, and released energy is written as a negative change
options.explanation: Burning fuels warm their surroundings, which fixes the sign by convention.

options.text: Because flames are hot, and hot means negative
options.explanation: The sign tracks energy flow, not temperature size.

options.text: Because fuels are negative chemicals
options.explanation: No chemical carries a sign; the transfer does.

options.text: Because kilojoules are always negative units
options.explanation: Units are neutral; endothermic values in kilojoules are positive.

questions.stem: Which order describes the reliable route through a heat energy calculation?

options.text: State the expression, list values, substitute, solve, apply the sign
options.explanation: That sequence keeps units and direction under control to the final line.

options.text: Guess the sign, substitute, then find the expression
options.explanation: The expression comes first; the sign is applied at the end from the temperature direction.

options.text: Convert to kilojoules first, then find the mass
options.explanation: The mass is needed before any multiplication can happen.

options.text: Solve, then decide which expression was used
options.explanation: Choosing the expression after solving makes the answer untraceable.

questions.stem: A student writes a positive answer although the mixture cooled. What went wrong?

options.text: The sign step was missed: a temperature fall means energy entered and the value is positive
options.explanation: The student should have ended with a positive value, so a negative one would show the opposite slip.

options.text: Nothing: cooling reactions always give positive numbers
options.explanation: The direction decides the sign; the student ignored it.

options.text: The mass must have been wrong
options.explanation: The described fault is the sign, not the mass.

options.text: The specific heat capacity should be negative for cooling
options.explanation: The capacity is a property of the substance and stays positive.

questions.stem: Q is calculated as 25080 J. Express this in kilojoules.

options.explanation: Dividing 25080 by 1000 gives 25.08, which rounds to 25.1 at three significant figures.
That divides by 100 rather than 1000.
That divides by a million, confusing joules with millijoules.
No conversion was applied at all.

questions.stem: State the sign carried by the heat energy change when the reaction mixture warms up.
questions.modelAnswer: A temperature rise shows an exothermic reaction, so the heat energy change must be given as negative.

questions.stem: State the conversion that turns Q in joules into kilojoules.
questions.modelAnswer: Dividing the value of Q by 1000 converts it from joules to kilojoules.

questions.stem: Explain why a perfect calculation without its negative sign still loses the chemistry for an exothermic answer.
questions.modelAnswer: The negative sign carries the chemistry, showing the system gave energy out to the surroundings; without it the answer reads as if energy flowed the wrong way.

questions.stem: A combustion calculation returns 4.5 kilojoules per gram of fuel. State the sign the final answer must carry and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Combustion is always exothermic, so the answer must be given as -4.5, showing energy released by the burning fuel.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the molar enthalpy change from the heat energy change?

options.text: It divides the heat energy change by the number of moles of fuel
options.explanation: The per-mole scaling is exactly what makes the value comparable between fuels.

options.text: It multiplies the heat energy change by the volume heated
options.explanation: Volume belongs to the mass step, and multiplication goes the wrong way.

options.text: It ignores the temperature change entirely
options.explanation: The temperature change feeds the heat energy change that the division starts from.

options.text: It is always measured directly by the thermometer
options.explanation: The thermometer only gives the temperature change; the molar value is calculated.

questions.stem: Which unit belongs to the molar enthalpy change?

options.text: kJ/mol
options.explanation: Kilojoules per mole is the stated unit for the molar enthalpy change.

options.text: J/°C
options.explanation: That mixes energy with a temperature step and misses the per-mole part.

options.text: g/J
options.explanation: That inverts both parts of the scaling.

options.text: mol/dm3
options.explanation: That is a concentration unit from a different topic.

questions.stem: 0.01 mol of a fuel warms water by an amount worth -12.54 kJ. What is the molar enthalpy change?

options.text: -1254 kJ/mol
options.explanation: Dividing -12.54 kJ by 0.01 mol scales the heat up to one mole.
That multiplies by 0.01 instead of dividing.

options.text: +1254 kJ/mol
options.explanation: The negative sign must survive the division.

options.text: -12.54 kJ/mol
options.explanation: No scaling by moles was applied.

questions.stem: Why compare fuels per mole rather than per experiment?

options.text: Different experiments burn different amounts, so only per-mole values are like for like
options.explanation: Scaling to a mole removes the effect of how much fuel happened to be burned.

options.text: Per-experiment values are always larger
options.explanation: Size depends on the amounts chosen, not on the basis of comparison.

options.text: Experiments are unreliable and should be avoided
options.explanation: The experiments are fine; the scaling is what makes them comparable.

options.text: Moles cancel the temperature change out
options.explanation: The temperature change still feeds the heat energy change at the start.

questions.stem: A fuel burns to release 20.9 kJ per gram. What additional data gives the molar enthalpy change?

options.text: The relative formula mass, to convert the per-gram value to a per-mole value
options.explanation: Multiplying the per-gram figure by the formula mass in g/mol reaches kJ/mol.

options.text: The volume of water heated
options.explanation: That data fed the original heat calculation and adds nothing here.

options.text: The colour of the flame
options.explanation: Flame appearance carries no quantitative information for this step.

options.text: The room temperature during burning
options.explanation: The temperature change is already inside the per-gram figure.

questions.stem: State how the energy released per gram of fuel is calculated.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy released per gram is the heat energy change divided by the mass of fuel burned.

questions.stem: State the unit carried by the molar enthalpy change.
questions.modelAnswer: The molar enthalpy change carries the unit kilojoules per mole, written kJ/mol.

questions.stem: Explain how the moles of fuel burned are found from its mass.
questions.modelAnswer: The mass of fuel is divided by its relative formula mass, converting grams into the number of moles burned.

questions.stem: Two fuels warm the same water beaker by different amounts, but one burned twice the mass of the other. State which quantities must be computed before the two fuels can be compared fairly.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy released must be scaled per gram or per mole for each fuel, so the fair comparison uses the energy per gram or the molar enthalpy change rather than the raw experiment totals.
